en.points: A man strains against the shafts of a handcart piled with bedding and household goods, hurrying through the rubble with a small child at his side; around him are the collapsed remains of burnt-out wooden houses, among which stand fire-scarred stone grave markers and broken Japanese shop signs, with tram rails in the foreground.
story: In the early hours of 10 March 1945, more than three hundred B-29s came in low over Tokyo's downtown districts on a northwest wind and dropped roughly half a million M69 incendiaries in a little over two hours. The wooden neighborhoods of Koto, Sumida and Taito burned to bare ground; forty-one square kilometers of the city vanished overnight and about one hundred thousand people died — the deadliest single air raid in the history of war. After dawn, the first thing the survivors did was drag whatever had not burned out of the ashes; the handcart in this photograph, heaped with bedding, clothing chests and cooking pots, is a miniature of that great exodus.

Koyo Ishikawa, who pressed the shutter, was a photographer at the Tokyo bureau of the Kochi Shimbun newspaper. On the morning of 10 March he rode his bicycle into fires that had not yet gone out, and photographed street after street while the embers were still hot, becoming one of the photographers who left the most images of the city on that very day. His photographs of victims, ruins and columns of the displaced were shown after the war in repeated exhibitions and photo books, and remain among the most important private records in the memory of the great Tokyo air raid.

In the photograph the stone grave markers and the hospital sign still stand where they were, and the tram rails run through the rubble — the city has lost its neighborhoods, but its old skeleton can still be made out. The bombing did not stop after 10 March: the night raids of 25 and 26 May burned away large residential stretches of Yamanote, and millions fled Tokyo. The handcart in this photograph was pushed from one district to the next, at the very head of the year of defeat.

title: 冲绳收容线
source: 美国陆军照片，1945年6月，冲绳本岛屋嘉部（一说屋比久）一带，冲绳县公文书馆藏（资料代码 0000112198）。画面要点：数十名被收容的冲绳平民在路旁歇脚，头顶包袱、肩挑行李，前方两名男子走过，背景是亚热带树丛与崩塌的石墙。
story: 1945年4月1日，美军在冲绳本岛西海岸登陆，约二十四万冲绳平民被卷入这场『铁暴风』。战斗向岛南部收缩的过程中，居民夹在日军阵地与炮火之间南逃，摩文仁、喜屋武一带的断崖前死伤枕藉；全战冲绳平民死亡约九万四千人，超过守军本身的损失。照片拍摄于战事接近尾声的6月：美军在占领区设置民间收容所，把陆续走出战场与洞穴的幸存居民集中起来，这张照片记录的就是被引往收容线途中的一队人。
照片由美国陆军随军摄影记录，战后由冲绳县公文书馆数字化公开。原始标注写明拍摄于1945年6月、地名『Yikabu』——对这两个音节的对应，研究者有屋嘉部与屋比久两种考订，冲绳战史研究者仲本和彦根据美军作战报告复原知念半岛战斗时，采屋比久之说。画面里的人们顶着包袱、挑着行李，赤足站在亚热带的土路边，身上还带着南部战线的泥。
收容所里有配给口粮、饮水与简易医疗，冲绳平民中的幸存者大半经由这里过渡到战后的生活。公文书馆在公开这批档案时逐一登记了资料代码与拍摄信息，使六十多年后的人们仍能循着一条影像线索，回到1945年6月那条通往收容线的土路。

en.title: Okinawan Civilians at the Collection Line
en.source: U.S. Army photograph, June 1945, in the Yagabu (by one account Yabiku) area of Okinawa Island; held by the Okinawa Prefectural Archives (item code 0000112198).
en.points: Dozens of collected Okinawan civilians rest at the roadside, bundles on their heads and luggage on shoulder poles; two men walk past in front, and behind them stand subtropical thickets and collapsed stone walls.
story: On 1 April 1945 American troops landed on the west coast of Okinawa Island, and some 240,000 Okinawan civilians were caught up in what came to be called the 'typhoon of steel.' As the battle shrank toward the south of the island, residents fled southward caught between Japanese lines and the bombardment, and the cliffs at Mabuni and Cape Kyan were strewn with the dead; over the whole battle about 94,000 Okinawan civilians died, exceeding the losses of the defending troops themselves. This photograph was taken in June, as the fighting neared its end: the Americans set up civilian camps in the occupied zones and gathered in the survivors as they came out of the battlefields and the caves, and this photograph records one party being led toward the collection line.

The photograph was taken by an accompanying U.S. Army photographer and digitized and released after the war by the Okinawa Prefectural Archives. The original caption gives June 1945 and the place-name 'Yikabu' — researchers are divided between Yagabu and Yabiku for those syllables, and Nakamoto Kazuhiko, a historian of the Battle of Okinawa, adopts Yabiku when reconstructing the fighting on the Chinen Peninsula from American operational reports. The people in the frame stand barefoot at the edge of a subtropical dirt road with bundles on their heads and luggage on shoulder poles, the mud of the southern front still on them.

In the camps there were rations, drinking water and basic medical care, and most of the surviving Okinawan civilians passed through them on their way into postwar life. When the Prefectural Archives released these materials it registered each item code and photographic detail, so that even more than sixty years later one can still follow a thread of images back to that dirt road leading to the collection line in June 1945.

title: 布干维尔投降行军
source: 澳大利亚昆士兰州立图书馆约翰·奥克斯利图书馆藏（编号 185551），1945年9月摄于布干维尔岛。一队日军士兵正沿土路行进，前往投降后的集合地点。画面要点：二十余名日军士兵列纵队迎面走来，着热带夏装、多缠头巾或戴战斗帽，背景是荒草地与热带丛林。
story: 布干维尔岛是所罗门群岛最北端的大岛。1943年11月美军在岛西岸托罗基纳登陆并建立庞大空军基地后，岛上的日本第十七军被压缩到南部一隅；1944年下半年起澳军第二军接替美军继续作战，经过1945年上半年沿岛屿轴线的一系列苦战，日军退路、补给尽断，靠挖掘木薯与野果苦撑。到战争结束时，这座岛上还困着约两万三千名日本官兵。
1945年8月15日玉音放送之后，停火的命令几经周折才传到这座与世隔绝的岛上。9月8日，第十七军军长神田正种中将在托罗基纳向澳军军长萨维奇中将正式投降，各部队随后放下武器、开往指定的收容地点。照片里这支沿土路走来的队伍，就是投降指令下达后前往集合点的日军部队：军装磨损、身形消瘦，但队列依然保持着行军的秩序。
这张照片由昆士兰州立图书馆的约翰·奥克斯利图书馆收藏，是澳军记录布干维尔受降过程的影像之一。对被俘的官兵而言，走完这条土路意味着三年半的岛屿战争终于到头；而对这座被战火烧秃的岛来说，这些疲惫的纵队，是它所承载的全部战事最后的收梢。

en.title: Surrender March on Bougainville
en.source: State Library of Queensland, John Oxley Library (No. 185551), photographed on Bougainville Island in September 1945. A column of Japanese soldiers marches along a dirt road toward its post-surrender assembly point.
en.points: Some twenty-plus Japanese soldiers march toward the camera in column, dressed in tropical summer uniforms, most with wrapped headcloths or field caps; the background is rough grassland and jungle.
story: Bougainville is the great northernmost island of the Solomons. After the Americans landed at Torokina on the west coast in November 1943 and built a vast air base there, the Japanese Seventeenth Army on the island was compressed into a southern corner; from the second half of 1944 the Australian II Corps took over from the Americans and kept pressing, and after a series of hard engagements along the island's axis in the first half of 1945 the Japanese were cut off from retreat and supply, surviving on dug cassava and wild fruit. When the war ended, some 23,000 Japanese officers and men were still trapped on the island.

After the Imperial broadcast of 15 August 1945, the ceasefire order reached this isolated island only after delays and detours. On 8 September Lieutenant General Masatane Kanda, commander of the Seventeenth Army, formally surrendered at Torokina to Lieutenant General Stanley Savige of the Australian corps, and the various units then laid down their arms and marched to the designated holding areas. The column coming along the dirt road in this photograph is one of those Japanese units on its way to the assembly point after the surrender order: uniforms worn thin, bodies gaunt, but the column still keeping its marching order.

The photograph is held by the John Oxley Library of the State Library of Queensland, one of the images by which the Australians recorded the surrender on Bougainville. For the officers and men taken prisoner, finishing this dirt road meant that three and a half years of island war had finally come to an end; for the island itself, burned bare by the war, these exhausted columns were the final winding-up of all the fighting it had carried.

title: 学童疏散列车
source: 中村立行摄于1945年，宫前国民学校学童再疏散列车的车厢内（自静冈滨松北上青森的漫长行程中），『学童集団疎開資料集』所收。画面要点：夜间车厢里，孩子们横在木座上沉沉睡去——一人仰面而眠，一人伏在椅背上——行李与布包挂在行李架上，窗外一片漆黑。
story: 1944年6月底，日本政府阁议决定『学童疏散促进要项』，把大都市无法托付亲戚的三至六年级学童以学校为单位送往地方，东京一地送出了约二十三万七千人。荏原区（今品川区）宫前国民学校的四百三十五名孩子，在1944年8月末离开大崎站，疏散到静冈县引佐郡奥山村的古刹方広寺，过起了寺院学寮的集体生活。

1945年5月24日东京南部空袭，宫前校校舍焚毁；静冈沿岸又被划为美军可能登陆的地带，学校接到再疏散的命令。6月1日下午，孩子们从滨松站登车北上：列车夜间经过品川，只停十分钟，闻讯赶来的父母在站台上呼喊孩子的名字，停车的十分钟一到，列车载着孩子继续北上，经奥羽本线走了四十多个小时才到弘前，再分散到津轻各地的学寮——去大鳄町的宫前校学童两百余人，住进了温泉旅馆改成的宿舍。这张照片就拍在这样一节夜行车的车厢里：孩子们横七竖八地睡在木座上，行李架上的布包随着车轮摇晃。
按下快门的中村立行（1912—1995）原是东京美术学校出身的小学图画教师，这次疏散中他以训导（随队教师）的身份全程引率，用相机记录下学寮生活、课堂、农事与旅途。这批底片战后由品川历史馆收藏整理，成为记录学童集体疏散最完整的一组私人影像。

en.title: The Schoolchildren's Evacuation Train
en.source: Photographed by Tatsuyuki Nakamura in 1945, inside a carriage of the re-evacuation train for the schoolchildren of Miyamae National School (on the long journey north from Hamamatsu, Shizuoka, to Aomori); collected in the 'Gakudo Shudan Sokai Shiryoshu' (documentary collection on the collective evacuation of schoolchildren).
en.points: In the night carriage the children lie fast asleep across the wooden benches — one on his back, another slumped over the seat back — bundles and cloth bags stowed on the luggage racks, the windows black outside.
story: At the end of June 1944 the Japanese cabinet decided on the program for promoting the evacuation of schoolchildren, sending third- through sixth-graders who could not be left with relatives off to the countryside school by school; Tokyo alone sent out about 237,000 children. In late August 1944 the 435 children of Miyamae National School in Ebara Ward (today's Shinagawa Ward) left Osaki Station for Hokoji, an ancient temple in Okuyama village, Inasa District, Shizuoka Prefecture, and began the collective life of a temple school dormitory.

In the air raid on southern Tokyo of 24 May 1945 the Miyamae school building burned down; the Shizuoka coast was then classified as a possible American landing zone, and the school received orders for a second evacuation. On the afternoon of 1 June the children boarded at Hamamatsu Station and headed north: the train passed through Shinagawa at night and stopped for only ten minutes, while parents who had heard the news called their children's names from the platform; when the ten minutes were up the train rolled on north with the children aboard, running more than forty hours by way of the Ou Main Line before reaching Hirosaki, where they were dispersed to school dormitories across the Tsugaru region — the two hundred-odd Miyamae children bound for Owani moved into a hot-spring inn converted into a dormitory. This photograph was taken in just such a carriage on the night run: the children sprawled asleep on the wooden benches, the cloth bags on the luggage racks swaying with the wheels.

Tatsuyuki Nakamura (1912–1995), who pressed the shutter, had trained at the Tokyo School of Fine Arts and was an elementary-school art teacher; throughout the evacuation he led the children as an accompanying teacher, recording dormitory life, lessons, farm work and the journeys with his camera. After the war his negatives were collected and arranged by the Shinagawa Historical Museum, and they remain the most complete private visual record of the collective evacuation of schoolchildren.

title: 香港街头的轻装甲车
source: 《香港岛上行驶的两辆九四式轻装甲车》（Two Japanese Type 94 tankettes were running on a street in Hong Kong Island），摄影师不详，摄于1941年12月26日香港陷落之后，香港岛商住街区；香港政府档案处「战争与占领」专题收录，公有领域。画面要点：低机位平视街景，前景右侧一辆九四式轻装甲车迎面驶来、乘员露身车外，中景左侧第二辆同型车斜向行驶、乘员舱处亦见露身者；左侧连排中式骑楼商住楼挂满繁体招牌，街道依山延伸、尽头停一辆卡车，左下骑楼柱廊下两名士兵随行；白昼顺光，玻璃底片划痕斑驳。
story: 1941年12月8日清晨，就在珍珠港遇袭的同一个日子，日军第23军越过深圳河进攻香港。守军在九龙半岛迟滞十二天后退守香港岛，18日夜日军渡海登陆，黄泥涌峡等地连日血战；12月25日下午，港督杨慕琦渡海到半岛酒店向日军投降——这一天被称作『黑色圣诞节』，历时十八天的香港战役结束，一万一千余名守军沦为战俘。
这张照片拍在香港陷落之后：一条挂满中文招牌的商住街区，两辆九四式轻装甲车前后驶过。九四式轻装甲车1934年定型，战斗全重约三吨半，乘员两人，只装机枪，是日军使用最广的侦察联络装甲车；车小履带窄，正适合在港岛的坡道窄巷里穿行。照片里乘员露身车外、士兵在骑楼柱廊下随行，街上行人绝迹——占领初期的香港街头就是这样。摄影师不详，这张照片由香港政府档案处『战争与占领』专题收录，属公有领域。
对香港来说，这十八天的终点是『三年零八个月』的起点：粮食配给、军票、归乡政策接踵而至，全港人口从沦陷时的约一百六十万减到1945年的六十万。骑楼上照常悬挂的繁体招牌与街心驶过的日军装甲车同框，是占领降临日常街市最直观的一帧影像。

en.title: Tankettes on a Hong Kong Street
en.source: 'Two Japanese Type 94 tankettes were running on a street in Hong Kong Island' (original caption), photographer unknown, taken after the fall of Hong Kong on 26 December 1941 in a commercial-residential street on Hong Kong Island; included in the Hong Kong Public Record Office's 'War and Occupation' collection, public domain.
en.points: A street scene at eye level from a low camera: in the right foreground a Type 94 tankette drives toward the camera with its crewmen riding exposed, and in the left middle distance a second vehicle of the same type moves obliquely with a man likewise visible at the crew compartment; on the left, a row of Chinese shophouse tenements hangs full of traditional shop signs, the street climbs with the hillside and ends at a parked truck, and two soldiers walk under the arcade columns at lower left; daylight frontal lighting, the glass negative heavily scratched.
story: At dawn on 8 December 1941, the same day as the attack on Pearl Harbor, the Japanese 23rd Army crossed the Sham Chun River and attacked Hong Kong. After delaying them on the Kowloon Peninsula for twelve days the defenders withdrew to Hong Kong Island; on the night of the 18th the Japanese crossed and landed, and bloody fighting continued for days at Wong Nai Chung Gap and elsewhere. On the afternoon of 25 December the Governor, Mark Young, crossed to the Peninsula Hotel to surrender to the Japanese — the day became known as 'Black Christmas'; the eighteen-day Battle of Hong Kong was over, and more than eleven thousand defenders became prisoners of war.

This photograph was taken after the fall of the city: on a commercial street hung with Chinese shop signs, two Type 94 tankettes drive past one after the other. The Type 94 light armored car was standardized in 1934, weighed about three and a half tons in combat order, carried a crew of two and mounted only machine guns — it was the most widely used Japanese scout and liaison armored vehicle, and its small hull and narrow tracks made it well suited to threading Hong Kong Island's slopes and lanes. In the photograph the crewmen ride exposed and soldiers walk beneath the arcade columns while not a civilian is in sight — such were the streets of Hong Kong in the first days of the occupation. The photographer is unknown; the image is in the Public Record Office's 'War and Occupation' collection and is in the public domain.

For Hong Kong, the end of those eighteen days was the beginning of 'three years and eight months': rationed food, military yen and the repatriation policy came one after another, and the population fell from about 1.6 million at the fall to 600,000 in 1945. The traditional shop signs hanging as always above the arcade, framed together with Japanese armored cars running down the middle of the street, make this the most direct image of occupation arriving in an everyday market street.

title: 西弗吉尼亚号救援
source: 美国海军官方照片，现藏美国国家档案馆，1941年12月7日上午摄于珍珠港。画面要点：一艘小型机动艇在满是浮油的水面上救人，艇上数名水兵正把落水舰员拉上船舷；燃烧的西弗吉尼亚号（BB-48）坐沉泊位，浓烟吞没上层建筑，高处两个小小的身影向小艇挥手，舰后内侧隐约可见田纳西号（BB-43）的桅杆。
story: 1941年12月7日晨7时55分，日本机动部队的舰载机突袭珍珠港。泊在『战列舰大街』最外侧的西弗吉尼亚号首当其冲，接连被多枚鱼雷与炸弹击中，左舷被撕开大口；舰长班宁在舰桥上被弹片击中，仍指挥损管直到阵亡，后被追授荣誉勋章。舰员们对称注水平衡舰体，让战舰平正地坐沉浅浅的港底，没有倾覆堵塞航道。大火烧了一天多，救生小艇在浮满重油的水面上一趟趟往返，这张照片记录的正是这样一次救援——燃烧的战舰旁，水兵把幸存者从水里拉上船；上层建筑高处还困着的舰员，正向小艇挥手示意。西弗吉尼亚号上共有106名舰员阵亡。
第二年打捞修复时，工人在舰体深处发现一间密闭舱室：里面的日历被划到12月23日。三名水兵靠淡水和应急口粮在黑暗里又活了十几天，却终究没能等到有人凿开那道舱壁。这个故事与救援小艇的照片一起，成为珍珠港最令人难以平静的记忆之一。
西弗吉尼亚号并没有就此终结：它被打捞起浮、彻底重建，1944年7月重返战场。当年10月，莱特湾海战的苏里高海峡夜战里，它用16英寸主炮为战列线领头开火，把西太平洋最后一批日本战列舰送进海底——珍珠港欠下的账，由同一艘船讨了回来。而这艘小艇在燃烧的战舰旁捞起幸存者的照片，则成了那一天流传最广的影像：灾难当头，救援没有停下。

en.title: Rescue Beside USS West Virginia
en.source: Official U.S. Navy photograph, held at the U.S. National Archives, taken on the morning of 7 December 1941 at Pearl Harbor.
en.points: A small motor boat picks up men from an oil-covered sea, sailors on board hauling soaked survivors over the gunwale; the burning USS West Virginia (BB-48) has settled to the harbor bottom in her berth, smoke swallowing her superstructure, and two tiny figures aloft wave to the boat — the masts of the Tennessee (BB-43) faintly visible inboard beyond her.
story: At 7:55 on the morning of 7 December 1941, carrier aircraft of the Japanese striking force fell upon Pearl Harbor. Moored on the outside of Battleship Row, USS West Virginia bore the first blows, hit by multiple torpedoes and bombs that tore open her port side; her captain, Mervyn Bennion, was struck by fragments on the bridge yet kept directing damage control until he died, and was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor. By counter-flooding, her crew kept the ship on an even keel as she settled upright to the shallow harbor bottom, so that she did not capsize and block the channel. The fires burned for more than a day, and boats shuttled back and forth across the water covered with heavy fuel oil; this photograph records one such rescue — sailors pulling survivors out of the water beside the burning ship, while men still trapped high on the superstructure wave to the boat. In all, 106 of West Virginia's crew were killed.

When the ship was salvaged and repaired the following year, workers deep in the hull found a sealed compartment: the calendar inside had been crossed off to 23 December. Three sailors had kept themselves alive on fresh water and emergency rations in the darkness for more than two weeks, but in the end no one broke through that bulkhead in time. Together with the photograph of the rescue boat, their story has remained one of the most haunting memories of Pearl Harbor.

West Virginia's war did not end there: she was raised, completely rebuilt, and returned to the battle line in July 1944. That October, in the night action in Surigao Strait during the Battle of Leyte Gulf, she led the battle line's opening fire with her 16-inch guns and helped send the last Japanese battleships in the western Pacific to the bottom — the debt of Pearl Harbor was repaid by the same ship. And the photograph of that little boat lifting survivors out of the water beside the burning battleship became one of the most widely circulated images of the day: in the midst of disaster, the rescue did not stop.

title: 杜立特空袭起飞
source: 美国海军官方照片（编号80-G-41196，现藏美国国家档案馆），1942年4月18日上午摄于太平洋。画面要点：一架陆军航空队B-25B米切尔轰炸机刚离开大黄蜂号（CV-8）的飞行甲板贴海爬升，起落架尚未收起，右侧信号灯平台上有数名戴钢盔的舰员凭栏眺望，海面翻涌、天色阴沉。
story: 1942年4月18日上午8时20分，距日本本土约650海里的洋面上，中校詹姆斯·杜立特驾驶的第一架B-25B从大黄蜂号湿滑的甲板上腾空——陆基中型轰炸机从航母甲板起飞，此前从未有人做过。舰队原计划驶到离岸400海里处再放飞机，但18日清晨被日本渔船日东丸发现，任务被迫提前十小时、在多出200海里的距离上仓促开始。16架B-25B每隔三四分钟一架依次滑出，到9时20分全部离舰，甲板上的水兵目送它们一架架贴着涌浪爬向西方。

因为提前起飞，机队几乎注定飞不到预定的中国机场：15架在中国东部沿海坠毁或迫降，机组多人在跳伞与迫降中受伤，3人丧生，8人被日军俘获——其中3人被处决、1人死于狱中；最后1架北飞苏联海参崴被扣留。落到浙江内陆的大多数队员被中国军民掩护转移，辗转回到盟军阵营。轰炸本身损失轻微，政治震动却难以估量：美国在连败数月之后第一次打击了日本本土，罗斯福总统对外笑称机队来自『香格里拉』；被激怒的日本海军随即发动中途岛攻势，6月在那一战中折损四艘航空母舰，太平洋战局从此逆转。
这张照片由美国海军摄影员在舰岛上拍摄，档案编号80-G-41196，照片说明特意注明『右侧信号灯平台上有人观望』——甲板上这些仰望的小小身影，与腾空的轰炸机一起，构成了整个杜立特空袭最著名的一帧。

en.title: Doolittle Raid Takeoff
en.source: Official U.S. Navy photograph (No. 80-G-41196, held at the U.S. National Archives), taken on the morning of 18 April 1942 in the Pacific.
en.points: An Army Air Forces B-25B Mitchell bomber has just left the flight deck of USS Hornet (CV-8) and climbs low over the sea, landing gear still down; several helmeted crewmen lean on the rail of the signal-flag platform at right watching it go, the sea rough under an overcast sky.
story: At 8:20 on the morning of 18 April 1942, about 650 nautical miles from the Japanese home islands, the first B-25B, flown by Lieutenant Colonel James Doolittle, lifted off the wet deck of Hornet — no land-based medium bomber had ever taken off from a carrier before. The task force had planned to steam to within 400 nautical miles of the coast before launching, but at dawn on the 18th it was spotted by the Japanese picket boat Nitto Maru, and the mission was thrown forward ten hours and begun hastily from 200 nautical miles farther out. The sixteen B-25Bs rolled out one after another at three- to four-minute intervals; by 9:20 all were airborne, and the sailors on deck watched them climb away low over the swells toward the west.

Because of the early launch, the formation had almost no chance of reaching the Chinese airfields as planned: fifteen aircraft crashed or crash-landed along the east China coast, many crewmen were injured bailing out or crash-landing, three were killed, and eight were taken by the Japanese — three of them executed and one dying in prison; the last aircraft flew north to Vladivostok in the Soviet Union and was interned. Most of the crews who came down over inland Zhejiang were sheltered and passed along by Chinese soldiers and civilians, eventually making their way back to the Allies. The bombing itself did little material damage, but the political shock was beyond measure: after months of defeat the United States had struck the Japanese home islands for the first time, and President Roosevelt quipped that the raiders had come from 'Shangri-La.' The enraged Japanese Navy launched the Midway offensive in response and lost four fleet carriers there in June; the war in the Pacific turned from that point.

This photograph was taken by a Navy photographer on the carrier's island, archived as 80-G-41196, and its caption specifically notes men watching from the signal-flag platform at right — those small figures gazing upward from the deck, together with the bomber clawing into the air, make up the most famous single frame of the entire Doolittle Raid.

title: 候车的日裔家庭
source: 多萝西娅·朗摄于1942年5月9日，加利福尼亚州森特维尔（美国国家档案馆藏，编号NARA 537577）。画面要点：带水塔的木板屋前，日裔农家一行人提着行李箱与包袱在路边列队候车，老人、妇女与孩子神情平静地等待把他们带走的大巴。
story: 1942年2月19日，罗斯福总统签署第9066号行政命令，授权军方把西海岸划为军事区；随后颁布的逐街驱逐令要求日裔居民在几天内变卖家产、只带随身行李报到。5月9日，森特维尔的第34号平民驱逐令生效：这个农业社区的全部595名日裔居民在自家屋前的路边列队，等候大巴把他们送到旧金山湾边的坦福兰集会中心——一座改作拘留营的赛马场，许多人住进了铺着稻草的马厩。多萝西娅·朗受战争救济管理局雇用，用相机记录下这个上午。
朗的照片没有回避她所见的不义：提着行李的普通人在自家门前排队，等一辆把他们全家带走的巴士。这些底片在战时被军方封存，藏进加州大学伯克利分校的班克罗夫特图书馆，战后多年才重见天日，成为这段历史最重要的一批影像记录。
从1942年春到战争结束，全美约12万日裔被强制迁移，其中约三分之二是美国公民。1944年最高法院在是松案里维持了驱逐令的合宪性，这个结论直到2018年才被正式否定；1988年，《公民自由法》由里根总统签署生效，美国政府向每位幸存的被拘押者正式道歉并赔偿两万美元。这张候车照片，是那场大规模迁离最平实的一帧注脚。

en.title: Japanese American Family Awaiting Evacuation
en.source: Photographed by Dorothea Lange on 9 May 1942 in Centerville, California (U.S. National Archives, NARA 537577).
en.points: In front of a wooden farm building with a water tower, a party of Japanese American farm families lines up at the roadside with suitcases and bundles, the old people, women and children waiting quietly for the bus that is to take them away.
story: On 19 February 1942 President Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066, authorizing the military to designate the West Coast a military zone; the civil exclusion orders that followed required Japanese American residents to sell off their property within days and report with only what they could carry. On 9 May Centerville's Civilian Exclusion Order No. 34 took effect: all 595 Japanese American residents of the farming community lined up at the roadside in front of their own homes to wait for buses to the Tanforan Assembly Center on San Francisco Bay — a racetrack converted into a detention camp, where many were housed in horse stalls bedded with straw. Dorothea Lange, employed by the War Relocation Authority, recorded that morning with her camera.

Lange's photographs did not turn away from the injustice she saw: ordinary people with their luggage, queuing in front of their own homes for a bus that would take their whole families away. Her negatives were impounded by the Army during the war and deposited at the Bancroft Library of the University of California, Berkeley; they only came to light years after the war and became one of the most important bodies of images documenting this history.

From the spring of 1942 to the end of the war, about 120,000 people of Japanese descent were forcibly relocated across the United States, roughly two-thirds of them American citizens. In 1944 the Supreme Court in the Korematsu case upheld the constitutionality of the exclusion orders, a holding not formally repudiated until 2018; in 1988 the Civil Liberties Act, signed by President Reagan, brought the U.S. government's formal apology and compensation of 20,000 dollars to each surviving internee. This photograph of people waiting for a bus is the plainest footnote to that mass removal.

title: 轰炸机尾段装配
source: 阿尔弗雷德·T·帕尔默摄于1942年10月，加利福尼亚州长滩的道格拉斯飞机公司工厂（国会图书馆FSA/OWI彩色透明片，编号fsac 1a35337）。画面要点：B-17F轰炸机的尾段机身内部，三名女工在一圈圈收拢的环形铝肋之间安装构件，机身蒙皮泛着冷银色的光。
story: 1942年10月，加州长滩的道格拉斯飞机公司工厂里，三名女工正在为一条B-17F『空中堡垒』的尾段机身安装构件：整流罩尚未蒙上，环形铝合金肋骨一圈圈收向机身深处，铆钉与卡口在灯下泛着银光。拍摄者阿尔弗雷德·帕尔默是农场安全管理局／战争情报局的摄影师，美国政府当年组织他用柯达彩色胶片系统记录后方的兵工厂，这批彩色透明片战后交存国会图书馆，成为二战美国后方最珍贵的一批彩色影像。
B-17F是『空中堡垒』的大改型，共造3405架：波音西雅图厂2300架，洛克希德维加厂500架，其余605架出自道格拉斯长滩厂——照片里的尾段正是其中之一。随着数百万男性穿上军装，美国飞机工业的工人里出现了大批妇女，铆枪与钻机声里的『铆工罗茜』成为那个年代最著名的形象；她们装配的每一架轰炸机要打上数万个铆钉，才能飞往欧洲与太平洋上空。
这张照片的构图几乎是一件工业时代的艺术品：人被围在金属的漩涡中央，安静、专注、看不见尽头。三年后战争结束时，一万两千余架B-17已从这样的车间飞向战场；而当年坐在尾段木箱上拧紧构件的女工们，与照片里的银色肋骨一起，留成了那个动员年代最光亮的注脚。

en.title: Assembling a B-17 Tail Section
en.source: Photographed by Alfred T. Palmer in October 1942 at the Douglas Aircraft Company plant in Long Beach, California (Library of Congress FSA/OWI color transparency, no. fsac 1a35337).
en.points: Inside the tail section of a B-17F bomber, three women workers install components among the rings of aluminum frames closing in toward the tail, the skin of the fuselage giving off a cool silver sheen.
story: In October 1942, at the Douglas Aircraft Company plant in Long Beach, California, three women workers are installing components in the aft fuselage of a B-17F Flying Fortress: the fairings are still uncovered, the aluminum frames ring inward toward the depth of the fuselage, rivets and fasteners gleaming silver under the lights. The photographer, Alfred Palmer, worked for the Farm Security Administration and the Office of War Information; the government commissioned him that year to record the home-front arsenals on Kodak color film, and these color transparencies were deposited at the Library of Congress after the war, becoming some of the most precious color images of the wartime American home front.

The B-17F was the heavily revised model of the Flying Fortress, of which 3,405 were built: 2,300 by Boeing in Seattle, 500 by Lockheed-Vega, and the remaining 605 by Douglas at Long Beach — the tail section in the photograph is one of them. As millions of men went into uniform, women came to make up a great share of the aircraft industry's workforce, and 'Rosie the Riveter', amid the whine of rivet guns and drills, became the most famous image of the age; every bomber they assembled carried tens of thousands of rivets before it could fly off to the skies over Europe and the Pacific.

The composition of this photograph is almost a work of industrial art: the workers are enclosed at the center of a whirl of metal, quiet, concentrated, with no end in sight. Three years later, when the war ended, more than twelve thousand B-17s had flown to the battlefields from workshops like this one; the women who once sat on crates inside the tail sections tightening fasteners remain, together with the silver frames in the photograph, among the brightest footnotes of that age of mobilization.

title: 塔拉瓦涉水登陆
source: 美国海军陆战队官方照片（陆战队档案馆Julian C. Smith收藏，COLL/202），1943年11月20日至23日塔拉瓦登陆期间摄于贝提奥岛近岸。画面要点：一长列陆战队员在齐腰的碎浪中涉水向岸，举着枪械与弹药，远处是登陆艇的轮廓与椰林岸线。
story: 1943年11月20日清晨，中太平洋反攻的第一战打响：陆战2师扑向塔拉瓦环礁的贝提奥岛。那是一道仅290英亩的珊瑚长岛，日军在岛上经营了一年多，工事密布。环绕小岛的珊瑚礁盘成了进攻最险恶的敌人：登陆艇在离岸500码处被珊瑚底搁住，只有首批两栖履带车能越过礁盘，后续各波官兵只得跳进齐胸的碎浪里，顶着纵深的交叉火力涉水数百码上岸——这张官方照片记录的正是那道长长的涉水队列，『不顾敌火，陆战队员涉过塔拉瓦岛外的碎浪』。
战斗持续了76小时。陆战队阵亡1009人、负伤2100余人，海军另有687人阵亡；约4800名守军中4690人战死，被俘的只有17名日军与129名朝鲜劳工。伤亡数字传回国内引起举国震动，国会与舆论追问代价是否值得。但塔拉瓦的经验很快显出分量：潮汐计算、两栖履带车、滩头组织与舰炮支援的每一个教训都被写进条令，一年后的塞班、再后的硫磺岛，都从这里起步。
随队登陆的陆战队摄影员拍下了整场血战，剪成纪录片《与陆战队在塔拉瓦》，赢得1945年的奥斯卡奖，也让美国公众第一次直视太平洋战场的真实代价。相比之下，这张涉水照片安静得多：碎浪的反光里，一列士兵把武器举过头顶，沉默地走向那座燃烧的岛。

en.title: Wading Ashore at Tarawa
en.source: Official U.S. Marine Corps photograph (Marine Corps Archives, Julian C. Smith Collection, COLL/202), taken offshore of Betio during the Tarawa landings of 20–23 November 1943.
en.points: A long line of Marines wades shoreward through waist-deep surf, holding rifles and ammunition above the water; in the distance are the silhouettes of landing craft and a palm-lined shore.
story: At first light on 20 November 1943 the Central Pacific counteroffensive opened its first battle: the 2nd Marine Division hurled itself at Betio islet in the Tarawa atoll. It was a coral sliver of barely 290 acres on which the Japanese had labored for over a year, thick with fortifications. The reef ringing the islet proved the deadliest enemy of the assault: the landing craft grounded on the coral 500 yards offshore, only the first waves of amphibian tractors could cross the reef, and the following waves of Marines had to jump into chest-deep surf and wade several hundred yards to the beach under interlocking fire from depth — this official photograph records that long wading line: Marines wade through the surf off Tarawa regardless of enemy fire.

The battle lasted 76 hours. The Marines lost 1,009 dead and over 2,100 wounded, and the Navy lost another 687 killed; of some 4,800 defenders, 4,690 were killed, and only 17 Japanese and 129 Korean laborers were taken prisoner. When the casualty figures reached home the whole country was shaken, and Congress and the press asked whether the price had been worth paying. But Tarawa's lessons soon showed their weight: tide calculations, amphibian tractors, beach organization and naval gunfire support — every lesson was written into doctrine, and Saipan a year later, and Iwo Jima after that, set out from here.

Marine combat photographers who landed with the division filmed the whole bloody battle, cut into the documentary 'With the Marines at Tarawa', which won an Academy Award in 1945 and let the American public look straight at the real cost of the Pacific war for the first time. By comparison this wading photograph is far quieter: in the glint of the surf a line of men holds its weapons overhead and walks in silence toward the burning islet.

title: 诺曼底篱田推进
source: 美国陆军通信兵照片（编号SC 191997），摄影员斯潘格尔，1944年7月25日摄于诺曼底。画面要点：第9步兵师第47步兵团第3营的士兵穿过推土坦克豁开的树篱缺口向前推进，翻掘的泥土、高大的橡树与弥漫的雾气之间，队伍沉默行进。
story: 诺曼底内陆的『波卡日』树篱地形，是1944年夏天盟军最难缠的对手之一：田埂用几百年挖起的土垒成，高过人头，顶上长满灌木与老树，把乡村割成一座座封闭的盒子。坦克找不到进出口，步兵的视野被压缩到几十米，德军的机枪与迫击炮守着每一条篱间小路；在这样的迷宫里，一天推进三百码就算顺利。
7月25日，美军发起『眼镜蛇』行动：千余架重型轰炸机沿佩里耶—圣洛公路一线轰炸德军防线。但当日南风把烟标吹偏，后一波炸弹落进了自己人的集结地，第9步兵师伤亡数百人，第47团第3营的营部几乎全体伤亡。轰炸过后，部队随即从推土坦克豁开的树篱缺口涌入，继续向南突击——通信兵摄影员斯潘格尔的这张照片，记下的正是第3营的士兵越过缺口的瞬间。
眼镜蛇的突破在几天内完成：7月底巴顿的第三集团军涌向阿夫朗什，8月盟军冲出诺曼底，德军在法莱斯被围歼。树篱战的僵持只有一个多月，却是西线最难走的一段路；照片里泥浆、浓雾与沉默前行的背影，替这场苦战留下了最贴切的注脚。

en.title: Advance Through the Norman Hedgerows
en.source: U.S. Army Signal Corps photograph (No. SC 191997), photographer Spangler, taken on 25 July 1944 in Normandy.
en.points: Soldiers of the 3rd Battalion, 47th Infantry Regiment, 9th Infantry Division push forward through a gap a bulldozer tank has torn open in the hedgerow; among the churned earth, tall oaks and drifting haze the column moves in silence.
story: The hedgerow country — the bocage — of inland Normandy was one of the Allies' most stubborn adversaries in the summer of 1944: the field banks, raised from centuries of digging, stood higher than a man's head and were topped with brush and old trees, cutting the countryside into sealed boxes. Tanks could find no way in or out, the infantry's field of view shrank to a few dozen meters, and German machine guns and mortars held every sunken lane between the hedges; in such a maze an advance of three hundred yards in a day counted as good going.

On 25 July the Americans launched Operation Cobra: over a thousand heavy bombers battered the German lines along the Periers–Saint-Lo road. But a south wind that day drifted the smoke markers, and the later waves of bombs fell on the Americans' own assembly areas; the 9th Infantry Division suffered several hundred casualties, and the headquarters of the 47th Regiment's 3rd Battalion was all but wiped out. Once the bombing ended, the troops poured through the gaps the bulldozer tanks had torn in the hedgerows and drove on south — this photograph by Signal Corps photographer Spangler records the moment the 3rd Battalion's soldiers crossed the breach.

Cobra's breakthrough was completed within days: at the end of July Patton's Third Army flooded toward Avranches, in August the Allies broke out of Normandy, and the German armies were encircled and destroyed at Falaise. The stalemate in the hedgerows had lasted barely a month, yet it was the hardest stretch of road in the West; the mud, the thick haze and the silent advancing backs in this photograph leave the most fitting footnote to that grim fight.

title: 塔斯克基装弹手
source: 美国陆军航空队官方照片（美国国家档案馆藏，编号208-MO-18H-32984），摄影托妮·弗里塞尔，1944年9月前后摄于意大利拉米泰利机场。画面要点：第332战斗机大队第100中队的一等兵约翰·菲尔茨跪在P-51B机翼上，正把12.7毫米机枪弹链送进翼上弹舱，身后机身写有机名Stinky。
story: 塔斯克基飞行员是美国陆军航空队第一批黑人飞行与地勤人员，因训练地阿拉巴马州塔斯克基而得名。在种族隔离尚未废除的军队里，这支部队必须用战绩证明自己：到1944年，本杰明·戴维斯上校指挥的第332战斗机大队已从北非转战意大利，7月起换装P-51野马，垂直尾翼涂上大队专属的鲜红识别带，被受护航的轰炸机乘员称为『红尾』。
拉米泰利机场是第15航空队的前进基地，出击目标是德国南方的炼油厂与铁路线。每次任务前，装弹员要把成串的12.7毫米机枪弹链送进机翼弹舱——P-51B每侧两挺、共四挺，枪口还要贴上胶带以防高空结冰卡壳。照片里的一等兵约翰·菲尔茨就是这样一名装弹手；为他按下快门的托妮·弗里塞尔是当时美国最著名的时尚摄影师之一，战时受军方委托赴意大利采访，拍下了这支部队最经典的一组影像。
332大队在二战中执行了两百余次轰炸护航任务，被护航的轰炸机因敌战斗机攻击造成的损失远低于其他护航部队的平均水平，战后『从未丢过一架轰炸机』的传说流传极广，后来的研究修正了这个数字，却没有动摇这支队伍的分量。1948年，杜鲁门总统签署第9981号行政命令废除军内种族隔离——塔斯克基飞行员用四年血战，成了这条路上最有力的证明。

en.title: A Tuskegee Armourer
en.source: Official U.S. Army Air Forces photograph (U.S. National Archives, No. 208-MO-18H-32984), photographed by Toni Frissell, taken around September 1944 at Ramitelli Airfield, Italy.
en.points: Private First Class John Fields of the 100th Fighter Squadron, 332nd Fighter Group, kneels on the wing of a P-51B feeding a belt of .50-caliber machine-gun ammunition into the wing ammunition bay; the name 'Stinky' is painted on the fuselage behind him.
story: The Tuskegee Airmen were the Army Air Forces' first Black pilots and ground crews, named for their training base at Tuskegee, Alabama. In a still-segregated service, the unit had to prove itself by its record: by 1944 the 332nd Fighter Group, commanded by Colonel Benjamin Davis, had fought its way from North Africa to Italy, and from July it re-equipped with P-51 Mustangs, their vertical tails painted the group's distinctive red — the bomber crews they escorted called them the 'Red Tails'.

Ramitelli was a forward base of the Fifteenth Air Force, striking at the refineries and rail lines of southern Germany. Before each mission the armourers fed linked belts of .50-caliber ammunition into the wing bays — the P-51B carried two guns per side, four in all, and the muzzles were taped over to keep them from icing up and jamming at altitude. Private First Class John Fields, in the photograph, was such an armourer; Toni Frissell, who photographed him, was one of America's best-known fashion photographers, sent to Italy on a wartime assignment for the military, and she took this unit's most celebrated series of images.

Over the war the 332nd Group flew more than two hundred bomber-escort missions, and the bombers it escorted lost far fewer aircraft to enemy fighters than the average of other escort groups; the postwar legend that it never lost a bomber spread wide, and later research corrected the number without shaking the standing of the unit. In 1948 President Truman signed Executive Order 9981 abolishing racial segregation in the armed forces — with four years of hard fighting behind them, the Tuskegee Airmen had become the most powerful proof on that road.

title: 巴斯托涅空投
source: 美国陆军通信兵照片，1944年12月26日摄于比利时巴斯托涅。画面要点：雪原上，第101空降师的士兵仰头望着掠过天际的C-47运输机编队，补给伞包正飘落，雪地间停着吉普与卡车，营房旁立着结霜的云杉。
story: 1944年12月16日，德军最后的战略反攻在阿登高原发起，五大交通枢纽之一的巴斯托涅成为双方必争之地。仓促调来的第101空降师与第9、第10装甲师分队退守城内，由麦考利夫准将统一指挥，从12月21日起陷入重围。22日德军递上劝降书，麦考利夫只回了一个词：『Nuts!』——『做梦！』。此后天公作难，浓雾封住天空，城内弹药与药品一天天见底。
23日起天气放晴，盟军的运输机群立刻压上：C-47在战斗机掩护下低空进入，伞投弹药、军械与医药，几天里送来上千吨物资。这张照片摄于12月26日：雪原上的士兵仰头数着飞来的机群，伞包从铅灰的天空里一朵朵飘下——就在同一天下午，巴顿第三集团军第4装甲师的坦克从南面突进巴斯托涅，围解。空中补给与那声『Nuts!』一起，成了这场围城战流传最广的两样遗产。
阿登战役是美军在二战中规模最大的单场地面战，阵亡约一万九千人，总伤亡逾八万。巴斯托涅守住了，德军的攻势在圣诞节前后失去势头，到1945年1月中被赶回出发线。这张空投照片里的雪原与仰望的身影，定格的是包围圈内的人们第一次望见转机的时刻。

en.title: Airdrop over Bastogne
en.source: U.S. Army Signal Corps photograph, taken on 26 December 1944 at Bastogne, Belgium.
en.points: Across a snowfield, soldiers of the 101st Airborne Division look up at a formation of C-47 transports passing overhead as supply bundles drift down on parachutes; jeeps and trucks stand in the snow, and frost-covered spruces stand by the barracks.
story: On 16 December 1944 the German army launched its last strategic counteroffensive in the Ardennes, and Bastogne — one of the region's five great road junctions — became ground both sides had to hold. The hastily moved-up 101st Airborne Division and elements of the 9th and 10th Armored Divisions fell back into the town under the unified command of Brigadier General Anthony McAuliffe, and from 21 December they were surrounded. On the 22nd the Germans delivered a note demanding surrender, and McAuliffe sent back a single word: 'Nuts!' Then the weather turned against the defenders: fog sealed the sky, and the town's ammunition and medicine ran lower day by day.

From the 23rd the sky cleared and the Allied transport fleets pressed in at once: C-47s came in low under fighter cover, parachuting ammunition, arms and medical supplies — more than a thousand tons over the following days. This photograph was taken on 26 December: soldiers on the snowfield count the incoming formations, supply bundles blossoming one by one from the lead-gray sky — and that same afternoon tanks of the 4th Armored Division of Patton's Third Army broke into Bastogne from the south, and the siege was lifted. The aerial resupply, together with that word 'Nuts!', became the two most enduring legacies of the siege.

The Battle of the Bulge was the largest single ground battle American forces fought in World War II: about nineteen thousand killed and more than eighty thousand total casualties. Bastogne held, the German offensive lost its momentum around Christmas, and by mid-January 1945 it had been thrown back to its start line. The snowfield and the upturned faces in this airdrop photograph fix the moment when the men inside the pocket first saw the tide turn.

title: 波罗的海机枪手
source: 《波罗的海舰队的高射机枪手》，红旗波罗的海舰队报纸随军摄影伊·德拉内什摄于1941年6月，爱沙尼亚凯拉车站附近，保卫塔林西南接近地的阵地上；刊于1941年6月25日《红色波罗的海舰队报》第148期。画面要点：中景平视，四联装M-4高射机枪架占据画面左侧，枪管群斜指左上，一名水兵伏在环形瞄准具后测瞄，右侧另一名水兵手握长操作杆望向枪口方向，背景是松树苗与开阔原野。
story: 照片刊登在1941年6月25日的舰队报纸《红色波罗的海舰队报》上——战争爆发才三天，德军飞机已经出现在波罗的海沿岸上空。阵地设在爱沙尼亚凯拉车站附近，掩护塔林的西南接近地。机枪架上是四挺7.62毫米马克沁重机枪并装的M-4高射机枪架，这种上世纪三十年代列装的武器专门用来对付低空进入的轰炸机与俯冲机。画面里操作机枪的两名红海军水兵都有名字：岸防炮兵高射机枪瞄准手维克托·古斯利亚罗夫，生于1920年；瞄准装定员辛亚温。分队由中校祖阿利什维利指挥。
入夏之后，北方集团军群的装甲部队横扫波罗的海三国，塔林在三面合围下苦撑到8月28日失守，波罗的海舰队突围撤往喀琅施塔得，一路在德军空袭与岸炮火力下损失惨重。古斯利亚罗夫没能走出这场退却：1941年8月，他在塔林地区被列为失踪。照片拍摄时没有人知道这些，两名水兵穿着夏季的白色帆布军服，神情专注地在枪架前各就各位——那是这座波罗的海之港被围前的最后一个夏天。
这张照片随着舰队报纸的排印机流传到舰队与岸防部队，战后由军事档案收藏，是卫国战争初期红海军岸防作战为数不多的清晰影像之一：四联机枪成排的枪管、水兵帽垂下的飘带与背后安静的松林，定格在战争刚刚落下的第一枚阴影里。

en.title: Baltic Fleet Anti-Aircraft Gunners
en.source: 'Anti-aircraft machine gunners of the Baltic Fleet', photographed in June 1941 by I. Delanesh, photographer with the newspaper of the Red Banner Baltic Fleet, on a position near Keila station, Estonia, covering the southwestern approaches to Tallinn; published in issue No. 148 of the fleet newspaper, 25 June 1941.
en.points: A middle-distance view at eye level: a quadruple M-4 anti-aircraft machine-gun mount fills the left of the frame, its barrels slanting toward the upper left; one sailor lies behind the ring sight taking aim, another at right grips the long operating lever and looks toward the muzzles, with young pines and open country behind.
story: The photograph appeared in the fleet newspaper on 25 June 1941 — only three days into the war, and German aircraft were already over the Baltic coast. The position stood near Keila station in Estonia, covering Tallinn's southwestern approaches. On the mount is the M-4, four 7.62mm Maxim heavy machine guns on a single anti-aircraft mount, a weapon adopted in the 1930s specifically against bombers and dive bombers coming in at low altitude. The two Red Navy sailors working the gun both have names: Viktor Guslyarov, the anti-aircraft machine-gun aimer of the coastal defense artillery, born 1920, and Sinyavin, the sight setter. The detachment was commanded by Lieutenant Colonel Zualishvili.

As the summer wore on, the armored forces of Army Group North swept across the three Baltic states; Tallinn held out hemmed in on three sides until it fell on 28 August, and the Baltic Fleet broke out for Kronstadt under constant German air attack and shore fire, losing heavily on the way. Guslyarov did not live through that retreat: in August 1941 he was listed as missing in the Tallinn area. No one knew any of this when the photograph was taken — the two sailors stand at their places at the mount in their summer white duck uniforms, absorbed in their task. It was the last summer before the encirclement of that Baltic port.

The photograph traveled with the fleet newspaper's presses to the fleet and the coastal defense forces, and after the war entered military archives; it is one of the few clear images of Red Navy coastal fighting from the opening period of the Great Patriotic War: the ranked barrels of the quadruple machine-gun mount, the ribbons streaming from the sailors' caps, and the quiet pine woods behind, fixed at the moment the war's first shadow fell.

title: 解放村庄的坦克
source: 《解放村庄中的坦克》，苏联新闻社战地摄影列昂尼德·巴特摄于1941年10月10日，东线一处刚获解放的村庄（俄新社存档照片第2551号，35毫米底片）。画面要点：平视全景，前导的T-26轻型坦克斜过画面左侧，车长立在炮塔舱口，第二辆坦克在道路右后方跟随，路旁木屋前几名村民驻足观望，地面留有积雪与车辙。
story: 1941年10月10日，战地摄影记者列昂尼德·巴特在一条村道上按下了快门：两辆涂着冬季白斑迷彩的苏军T-26轻型坦克沿村道驶过，车长从炮塔舱口探出半个身子，路旁木屋前的村民远远望着这支小小的装甲纵队。照片作为苏联新闻社的战地报道底片留存下来，如今藏于俄新社影像档案。

这是战争爆发后的第一个秋天。德军『台风』行动在10月初重启对莫斯科方向的攻势，维亚济马方向的天塌了下来，前线在泥泞与初雪中向西退去；也正是在这样的日子里，苏军仍在个别地段发起局部反突击，把村庄从德军手中夺回来——照片里这支坦克分队，就是这类反击的参与者。1941年的第一场雪恰在10月上旬落下，泥泞的乡间土路一夜之间冻上白霜，坦克乘员往装甲上刷出雪斑迷彩，好在这片原野很快就会变成一片白色，把自己藏进去。
巴特是苏联新闻社与塔斯社摄影记者体系的随军摄影之一，以1941年秋冬西方向的战地照片为人所知，后来拍下的解放克林等影像同样出自这个时期。这张小小的村道照片没有波澜壮阔的构图，却记下了战争最严酷的一个秋天里极少被拍下的东西：刚刚回家的村民，和替他们把家夺回来的士兵。

en.title: Tanks in a Liberated Village
en.source: 'Tanks in a liberated village', a Soviet Information Bureau war photograph by Leonid Bat, taken on 10 October 1941 in a just-liberated village on the Eastern Front (RIA Novosti archive photograph No. 2551, 35 mm negative).
en.points: An eye-level panoramic view: the lead T-26 light tank crosses obliquely on the left of the frame, its commander standing in the turret hatch; a second tank follows on the road behind at right; several villagers stand watching before the log houses along the road, and the ground holds snow and track marks.
story: On 10 October 1941 the war photographer Leonid Bat pressed the shutter on a village road: two Soviet T-26 light tanks daubed with winter whitewash camouflage roll down the lane, the tank commander half out of his turret hatch, and villagers before the log houses watch the little armored column from a distance. The photograph survives as a Soviet Information Bureau combat-report negative and is now held in the RIA Novosti photo archive.

It was the first autumn of the war. In early October the German Operation Typhoon renewed the drive on Moscow, the front caved in along the Vyazma axis, and the lines retreated west through mud and the first snows; yet even in those days Soviet forces still mounted local counter-blows on individual sectors, taking villages back from the Germans — the tank detachment in the photograph took part in just such a counterattack. The first snow of 1941 fell in the first ten days of October; the muddy country roads froze white overnight, and tank crews dabbed snow-spot camouflage onto their armor, so that when the open country soon turned entirely white the machines would melt into it.

Bat was one of the staff war photographers of the Soviet Information Bureau and TASS system, known for his photographs from the western direction in the autumn and winter of 1941; his later images of the liberation of Klin likewise belong to this period. This small village-road photograph has no sweeping composition, yet it recorded something almost never caught in that hardest autumn of the war: villagers just returned home, and the soldiers who had won their homes back for them.

title: 红十月工人营
source: 《红十月工厂区的工人营战士》，苏联新闻社摄影记者埃马纽埃尔·叶夫泽里欣摄于1942年10月，斯大林格勒『红十月』钢铁厂附近射击线上；前景为工厂工人支队班长瓦西里·莫吉利林（1908年生，原车工）。画面要点：低机位近景，四名头戴钢盔的工人民兵在瓦砾间卧姿举枪，枪口指向同一方向，前景一人背对镜头大比例入画，远景厂区轮廓升起浓烟。
story: 1942年10月，斯大林格勒的工厂区正被打成齑粉。『红十月』钢铁厂的工人营在厂区西侧的射击线上占据了阵地：照片里四名民兵戴着SSh-40钢盔，在瓦砾、碎砖与歪斜的铁轨之间卧倒举枪，枪口一齐指向德军来袭的方向。离镜头最近的那名班长得上了名字——瓦西里·伊万诺维奇·莫吉利林，1908年生，战前是厂里的车工，此刻是并入近卫第39步兵师序列的工厂工人支队班长。

1942年8月23日，德军第四装甲集团军突抵伏尔加河，当天的大空袭把这座居民约四十万的城市烧成一片火海；从那天起，还没来得及后撤的工厂工人们拿起武器，编成了一个个工人营。9月末起，崔可夫的第62集团军背水据守河岸最后的狭长地带，近卫第39师于10月初进入『红十月』厂区，工人们与他们并肩守在车间之外几百米的散兵线上——平炉的火光就在身后，战线有时近到可以从车间直接看到德军的位置。叶夫泽里欣就是在这样的阵地上拍到这张照片的：民兵们身上的多是杂色的便服与棉衣，只有钢盔和手里的莫辛步枪表明他们已经不再是工人。
叶夫泽里欣是苏联新闻社的摄影记者，1942年8月他在斯大林格勒拍下了著名的儿童旋转木马喷泉废墟照，此后整个会战期间始终留在城里。这张工人营的照片是那段历史最直接的注脚：这座城市最初的一批守卫者，不是被派来的，是他们自己没有走。

en.title: The 'Red October' Workers' Battalion
en.source: 'Fighters of the workers' battalion in the Red October factory district', by Soviet Information Bureau photographer Emmanuil Yevzerikhin, taken in October 1942 on the firing line near the Krasny Oktyabr (Red October) steelworks in Stalingrad; in the foreground, squad leader Vasily Mogilin of the factory workers' detachment (born 1908, a lathe operator in civilian life).
en.points: A close view from a low camera: four helmeted workers' militiamen lie among the rubble with rifles raised, muzzles all pointing the same way; one man fills the foreground with his back to the camera, and the silhouette of the factory district rises in smoke beyond.
story: In October 1942 Stalingrad's factory district was being pounded to dust. The workers' battalion of the Krasny Oktyabr steelworks held positions on the firing line west of the plant: in the photograph four militiamen in SSh-40 helmets lie among rubble, broken brick and buckled rails with their rifles up, muzzles all trained in the direction of the German attacks. The squad leader closest to the camera has come down to us by name — Vasily Ivanovich Mogilin, born 1908, before the war a lathe operator at the plant, now a squad leader in the factory workers' detachment incorporated into the 39th Guards Rifle Division.

On 23 August 1942 the German Fourth Panzer Army reached the Volga, and the great air raid that day burned this city of some four hundred thousand into a single sheet of fire; from that day the factory workers who had not been evacuated took up arms and were formed into workers' battalions. From late September Chuikov's 62nd Army held its last narrow strip along the river bank, and in early October the 39th Guards Rifle Division moved into the Krasny Oktyabr plant, with the workers holding the skirmish line a few hundred meters beyond the shop floors beside them — the open-hearth furnaces glowing at their backs, and the front at times so close that the German positions could be seen directly from the shops. It was on such a position that Yevzerikhin took this photograph: the militiamen mostly wear mixed civilian clothes and padded jackets, and only the helmets and the Mosin rifles in their hands show that they are workers no longer.

Yevzerikhin was a Soviet Information Bureau photographer; in August 1942 he took the famous picture of the ruined children's carousel fountain in Stalingrad, and he stayed in the city through the entire battle. This photograph of the workers' battalion is the most direct footnote to that history: the city's first defenders were not sent there — they were the ones who simply did not leave.

title: 沃尔霍夫医院
source: 《野战医院，沃尔霍夫方面军，1943》，苏联摄影记者安纳托利·加拉宁摄于1943年1月13日，沃尔霍夫方面军地段（俄新社存档照片第662767号）。画面要点：中景平视，雪地松林的空地上支着两顶大型帆布手术帐篷，几名穿白色围裙的医护人员抬着担架走向帐篷，担架上伤员盖着军大衣，雪地上留着一串脚印。
story: 1943年1月13日，『火花』行动发起的第二天。前一天上午，沃尔霍夫方面军与列宁格勒方面军在拉多加湖南岸同时发起猛攻，要撕开已经围困列宁格勒一年半的封锁圈。沃尔霍夫方面军地段的森林里，野战医院就设在离前线不远处的雪地空地上：两顶巨大的帆布帐篷撑在松林之间，伤员被源源不断地从冲击出发线上抬下来。照片里，几名系着白围裙的医护人员正抬着担架走向帐篷，伤员身上盖着厚厚的军大衣，脚下的雪地里踩出一串深深的脚印。
这一仗打了六天。1月18日，两路红军在锡尼亚维诺以东的工人村会师，拉多加湖南岸被撕开一条8至11公里宽的走廊，被围的列宁格勒重新有了陆上出口；随即在炮火下抢建什利谢利堡铁路，17天后通车——列宁格勒人叫它『胜利之路』。打通走廊的代价是双方数以万计的伤亡，这些伤员中的许多人，正是被照片里这样的担架队从雪地里一步步抬回生命的。
拍摄者安纳托利·加拉宁是苏联的老一辈摄影记者，战时在多个方向随军采访。这张照片最动人处在于它的克制：没有血迹，没有喊叫，白围裙与白雪几乎融成一体，只有担架的姿态说明这里刚刚经历了什么。它是『火花』行动留下的最著名的影像之一。

en.title: Field Hospital, Volkhov Front
en.source: 'Field hospital, Volkhov Front, 1943', by Soviet photographer Anatoly Garanin, taken on 13 January 1943 in the Volkhov Front sector (RIA Novosti archive photograph No. 662767).
en.points: A middle-distance view at eye level: two large canvas surgical tents are pitched in a clearing among snowy pines; several medical workers in white aprons carry a stretcher toward the tents, the wounded man beneath a greatcoat, a line of footprints trailing through the snow.
story: 13 January 1943, the second day of Operation Iskra ('Spark'). The previous morning the Volkhov and Leningrad Fronts had attacked simultaneously on the southern shore of Lake Ladoga, aiming to tear open the ring that had blockaded Leningrad for a year and a half. In the forests of the Volkhov Front sector the field hospital stood in a snow clearing not far from the front line: two enormous canvas tents pitched among the pines, with the wounded carried down without pause from the jump-off positions. In the photograph, medical workers in white aprons carry a stretcher toward the tents, the wounded man under a thick greatcoat, deep footprints pressed into the snow behind them.

The battle lasted six days. On 18 January the two Soviet spearheads met at the workers' settlement east of Sinyavino, and an 8-to-11-kilometer-wide corridor was torn open along the southern shore of Lake Ladoga, giving blockaded Leningrad a land exit once more; the Shlisselburg railway was then built under shellfire and opened seventeen days later — the people of Leningrad called it the 'Road of Victory'. The cost of the corridor was tens of thousands of casualties on both sides, and many of these wounded were carried back to life, step by step through the snow, by stretcher teams like the one in this photograph.

Anatoly Garanin, who took it, was of the older generation of Soviet photojournalists and covered the war with the troops on several fronts. The photograph's power lies in its restraint: no blood, no crying out, the white aprons nearly melting into the white snow — only the posture of the stretcher says what has just happened here. It is one of the best-known images left by Operation Iskra.

title: 斯大林格勒攻坚
source: 《攻坚》，苏联摄影记者格奥尔基·泽尔马摄于1943年2月，斯大林格勒市区（俄新社存档照片第44732号，6×6底片）。画面要点：宽幅全景，成排的残破楼群横在硝烟里，数名士兵分成两三组越过瓦砾坡向前突进，前景碎砖垒起的高台上也有人影伏定。
story: 1943年2月，斯大林格勒的反攻已进入最后阶段。被合围在城中的德军第6集团军在『指环』行动的连续打击下只剩残破的一角：1月31日保卢斯在南部陷落的百货商店地下室被俘，2月2日北部工厂区的最后一批守军放下武器。泽尔马的这张宽幅照片拍下的正是巷战最后的样子——从这个秋天起，崔可夫的第62集团军就把这种打法磨成了教科书：工兵、冲锋枪手与掷弹兵编成突击组，沿街道两侧的断墙跃进，一组掩护、一组突进，一个房间一个房间地凿穿一栋楼。照片里越过瓦砾坡的几名士兵正是这样的突击组，远处的成排楼群已经没有一扇完整的窗。
泽尔马1906年生于季拉斯波尔，1920年代起做摄影记者，是苏联最出色的战地摄影家之一。从1942年8月德军突抵伏尔加，到1943年2月全城停火，他始终在斯大林格勒，拍下这座会战最完整的一批影像；此后的库尔斯克与柏林，也都有他的快门。他的斯大林格勒照片在战后多次展出，成为这场会战在世界记忆里的基本画面。
这张照片的视线尽头没有胜利的旗帜，只有硝烟里沉默的楼群——但2月初过去之后，这座城市成了整个战争的转折点：德军损失了整个第6集团军与并肩部队的各个分队，从伏尔加河到柏林，红军此后再没有退回去。

en.title: The Assault in Stalingrad
en.source: 'The assault', by Soviet photojournalist Georgy Zelma, taken in February 1943 in the city of Stalingrad (RIA Novosti archive photograph No. 44732, 6x6 negative).
en.points: A wide panorama: rows of shattered buildings lie across the smoke haze, several soldiers in two or three groups dash forward over the slopes of rubble, and on the high platform of broken brick in the foreground figures lie prone in position.
story: By February 1943 the counteroffensive at Stalingrad had entered its final stage. The encircled German Sixth Army, ground down by the successive blows of Operation Ring, was reduced to a ragged corner of the city: on 31 January Paulus was captured in the basement of the department store in the collapsing southern pocket, and on 2 February the last defenders in the northern factory district laid down their arms. Zelma's wide-frame photograph shows street fighting in its final form — since the previous autumn, Chuikov's 62nd Army had polished this method into a textbook: sappers, submachine gunners and grenadiers combined into assault groups, leapfrogging along the broken walls on either side of a street, one group covering while another advanced, cutting through a building one room at a time. The soldiers crossing the rubble slope in the photograph are just such an assault group, and not one intact window remains in the rows of buildings beyond.

Zelma was born in Tiraspol in 1906 and worked as a photojournalist from the 1920s, one of the finest Soviet war photographers. From the German breakthrough to the Volga in August 1942 to the final ceasefire in the ruined city in February 1943 he was in Stalingrad throughout, taking the most complete photographic record of the battle; his shutter was heard again later at Kursk and Berlin. His Stalingrad photographs were exhibited many times after the war and became the fundamental images of the battle in the world's memory.

At the far end of this photograph's gaze there is no banner of victory, only the silent rows of buildings in the smoke — but once the first days of February had passed, the city had become the turning point of the entire war: Germany lost the whole Sixth Army and the units that fought beside it, and from the Volga to Berlin the Red Army never again fell back.

title: 狙击手分队
source: 《行军途中的苏军狙击手分队》，战地摄影记者帕维尔·特罗什金摄于1943年，中央方面军（军事照片档案 waralbum.ru 编号52373）。画面要点：中景平视，狙击手纵队沿野地行进，数十支莫辛步枪成排斜扛肩上，人人头戴船形帽，前景一名年轻狙击手侧脸清晰。
story: 1943年春夏，中央方面军的地段上，一队狙击手沿着野地行军：莫辛步枪一支挨一支地斜扛在肩上，枪口朝天，枪背带垂着，人人戴着船形帽、穿着洗旧的军便服。队里有老练的面孔，也有少年气的新兵——队列后排一名来自东部地区的年轻狙击手眉目沉静。照片署名帕维尔·特罗什金，藏于战时照片档案。
狙击作战在这条战线上已经打成了系统：从列宁格勒城下的狙击运动，到斯大林格勒的瓦砾堆，两三年的消耗让红军把狙击手编成分队成建制使用，靠狙击学校成批培养，老手带新手上前沿『实习』，猎杀之间还要判风、判光、判距离。照片里枪口统一朝上的行军队列正是这种专业化的细节——枪口朝天是行军纪律，为的是走远路时不磕碰瞄准装置，也是不掉队、不出声的队列规矩。
拍摄者特罗什金1909年生，《消息报》的随军摄影记者，1939年在哈拉哈河拍过诺门罕战役，卫国战争爆发后从第一天起就在前线，与作家康斯坦丁·西蒙诺夫长期同行，1944年牺牲。他留下的这份底片里，那一代狙击手稚气未脱的脸和身后空旷的原野，是他们走向库尔斯克北麓之前留下的合影。

en.title: A Sniper Detachment on the March
en.source: 'A Soviet sniper detachment on the march', by war photographer Pavel Troshkin, taken in 1943 with the Central Front (war photo archive waralbum.ru, No. 52373).
en.points: A middle-distance view at eye level: a column of snipers advances across open fields, dozens of Mosin rifles slanted in rows across their shoulders; every man wears a side cap, and in the foreground a young sniper's profile is sharply visible.
story: In spring and summer 1943, in the Central Front sector, a detachment of snipers marches across open country: Mosin rifles carried muzzle-up, one against the next across their shoulders, slings hanging loose, every man in a side cap and a washed-out service shirt. There are seasoned faces in the ranks and boyish recruits too — in the rear of the column a young sniper from the eastern regions looks out with a calm, steady face. The photograph is signed by Pavel Troshkin and held in a wartime photo archive.

By then sniping on this front had become a system: from the sniper movement before Leningrad to the rubble heaps of Stalingrad, two or three years of attrition had led the Red Army to organize snipers into complete detachments, trained in batches at sniper schools, with veterans taking recruits up to the forward edge for their apprenticeship, learning to judge wind, light and distance between kills. The column in the photograph, every muzzle uniformly skyward, is a detail of that professionalism — muzzles up was marching discipline, to keep the sights from being knocked about on a long march, and a rule of column order: keep up, keep silent.

Troshkin, born 1909, was a war photographer of Izvestia; he had covered the Battle of Khalkhin Gol on the Khalkha River in 1939, was at the front from the first day of the Great Patriotic War, worked for long stretches alongside the writer Konstantin Simonov, and was killed in 1944. In the negatives he left behind, the still-boyish faces of that generation of snipers and the empty fields stretching behind them are the group portrait they left before setting out for the northern shoulder of Kursk.

title: 飞行员与空中眼镜蛇
source: 《第21近卫歼击航空团的飞行员们在克拉斯诺亚尔斯克机场的P-39『空中眼镜蛇』旁》，塔斯社摄影记者斯捷潘·马洛比茨基摄于1943年5月，克拉斯诺亚尔斯克机场。画面要点：中景平视，两三名穿深色飞行服的飞行员立于画面左前景，一人抬手指向战机，机身上有『克拉斯诺亚尔斯克工人』白色机铭，桨叶与机头在画面右中部。
story: 1943年5月，克拉斯诺亚尔斯克机场，几名飞行员站在一架崭新的贝尔P-39『空中眼镜蛇』旁：机身上用白漆写着这架飞机的名字——『克拉斯诺亚尔斯克工人』。这架战斗机是用克拉斯诺亚尔斯克边疆区劳动者的捐款购得的，共十架，全部交给正在当地整编的近卫第21歼击航空团；照片里左起第二人是该团指挥员、近卫上尉维克托·雅基莫夫。随行的塔斯社摄影记者斯捷潘·马洛比茨基拍下了交付后的这一幕。
『空中眼镜蛇』是租借法案下苏联飞行员最钟爱的美制战机：37毫米机炮从螺旋桨桨毂中穿出，发动机装在飞行员座舱之后，低空与中空性能出色。苏联是这种战机最大的使用国，总计接收约4700架，其中大半沿着阿拉斯加—西伯利亚空中航线飞抵——这条从费尔班克斯出发、穿越整个西伯利亚的转场航线全程数千公里，克拉斯诺亚尔斯克正是航线上的关键基地之一。波克雷什金、列奇卡洛夫等头号王牌都在『眼镜蛇』上创下了大部分战绩。
照片里立着的飞行员们几个月后将带着这些飞机回到前线。捐赠飞机是战时全国募捐运动的一部分——工厂、集体农庄与报社各自凑钱认捐，机身上的名字就是捐助者的署名；『克拉斯诺亚尔斯克工人』报的读者们买下的这十架战机，就这样带着一座城市的名字飞上了前线。

en.title: Pilots and the Airacobra
en.source: 'Pilots of the 21st Guards Fighter Aviation Regiment beside a P-39 Airacobra at Krasnoyarsk airfield', by TASS photographer Stepan Malobitsky, taken in May 1943 at Krasnoyarsk airfield.
en.points: A middle-distance view at eye level: two or three pilots in dark flying suits stand in the left foreground, one raising a hand toward the aircraft, whose fuselage carries the white dedication 'Krasnoyarsk Worker'; propeller blades and nose occupy the middle right of the frame.
story: May 1943, Krasnoyarsk airfield: several pilots stand beside a factory-fresh Bell P-39 Airacobra, its name painted in white on the fuselage — 'Krasnoyarsk Worker'. The fighter was bought with donations from the working people of Krasnoyarsk Krai; ten of them in all were handed over to the 21st Guards Fighter Aviation Regiment, then re-forming in the area. Second from the left in the photograph is the regiment's commander, Guards Senior Lieutenant Viktor Yakimov. Stepan Malobitsky, the TASS photographer accompanying the delivery, took the scene.

Under Lend-Lease the Airacobra was the American fighter Soviet pilots loved best: a 37mm cannon firing through the propeller hub, the engine mounted behind the cockpit, and outstanding performance at low and medium altitude. The USSR was the type's largest user, receiving about 4,700 in all, more than half of them flown in along the Alaska–Siberia air route — a ferry route thousands of kilometers long, starting at Fairbanks and crossing all of Siberia, with Krasnoyarsk one of its key staging bases. Leading aces such as Pokryshkin and Rechkalov scored most of their victories in the Airacobra.

The pilots standing in the photograph would take these machines back to the front a few months later. Donated aircraft were part of the nationwide wartime fund-raising drive — factories, collective farms and newspapers each pooled money to sponsor aircraft, and the name on the fuselage was the sponsor's signature; the ten fighters bought by the readers of the Krasnoyarsk Worker newspaper flew to the front carrying the name of an entire city.

title: 矿工游击队
source: 《克里沃罗格矿工游击队返回解放的城市》，苏联摄影记者以色列·奥泽尔斯基摄于1944年2月，乌克兰克里沃罗格。画面要点：中景平视，十余名游击队员聚集在一栋砖楼前的雪地上，装束杂色，一人抱捷格加廖夫转盘机枪，数人持步枪，弹药链斜挎胸前，中央一人抬手指挥。
story: 1944年2月，乌克兰第3方面军沿第聂伯河右岸发起尼科波尔—克里沃罗格攻势，2月22日解放了克里沃罗格——这座以铁矿闻名的工业城市在德军占领下熬过了两年半。就在红军进城的日子里，一张照片被拍了下来：克里沃罗格的矿工游击队返回了解放的城市。十余名队员聚在一栋砖楼前的雪地上，穿的还是离开矿井时的杂色冬装，棉帽、便帽与军帽混戴，肩上背着步枪，中间一人怀里抱着一挺捷格加廖夫转盘机枪，弹药链斜挎在棉衣外——这是游击队最典型的武装模样。
占领期间，德占领者急欲恢复克里沃罗格铁矿区的开采以支撑战争经济，而这里的抵抗恰恰来自最懂矿的人：矿工们消极怠工、破坏设备、让矿井灌水，地下组织传递情报、组织怠工，被搜捕的积极分子退入林中打游击。两年半里矿区被反复戒严与清剿，游击队的成员名单就是一张矿工与冶金工人的名册。当红军重新打到城下时，他们随军回到了自己的街区。
拍摄者以色列·奥泽尔斯基（1904–1971）是战时活跃在乌克兰方向的苏联摄影记者，拍下过右岸乌克兰诸城解放的许多影像。这张合影式的照片里没有激战，只有一群重新站上自家门前雪地的人：他们把机枪抱在怀里，把步枪靠在腿边，像下班时等工牌那样站着——只是矿井与街道都已面目全非。

en.title: The Miner Partisans of Krivoy Rog
en.source: 'Krivoy Rog miner partisans return to the liberated city', by Soviet photojournalist Israel Ozersky, taken in February 1944 in Krivoy Rog, Ukraine.
en.points: A middle-distance view at eye level: a dozen or more partisans gather on the snow in front of a brick building in mixed dress; one man holds a Degtyarev pan-magazine light machine gun, several carry rifles with ammunition belts slung across their chests, and the man at the center raises a hand to direct them.
story: In February 1944 the 3rd Ukrainian Front launched the Nikopol–Krivoy Rog offensive along the right bank of the Dnieper and liberated Krivoy Rog on 22 February; the industrial city famed for its iron ore had endured two and a half years of German occupation. In the very days the Red Army entered the city, this photograph was taken: the miner partisans of Krivoy Rog returning to their liberated city. A dozen or more of them gather on the snow in front of a brick building, still in the mixed winter clothes they wore when they left the mines — quilted hats, civilian caps and service caps worn together, rifles on shoulders, one man in the middle cradling a Degtyarev pan-magazine light machine gun with its ammunition belt slung over his padded jacket — the most typical look of a partisan's armament.

During the occupation the Germans were eager to restart mining in the Krivoy Rog iron basin to feed their war economy, and resistance there came precisely from the men who knew the mines best: the miners slowed their work, sabotaged equipment and let the shafts flood; the underground passed on intelligence and organized go-slows; and activists hunted by the police withdrew into the forests to fight as partisans. Across two and a half years the mining district was repeatedly placed under martial law and swept by punitive raids, and the partisan rosters were literally lists of miners and metallurgical workers. When the Red Army fought its way back to the city, they returned with it to their own streets.

Israel Ozersky (1904–1971), who took the photograph, was a Soviet photojournalist active on the Ukrainian fronts and recorded the liberation of many cities of the Right-Bank Ukraine. There is no battle in this group portrait — only men standing once more on the snow outside their own homes: the machine gun cradled in their arms, rifles propped against their legs, standing as if waiting at the pit-head for their tally tags — only the mines and the streets themselves were changed beyond recognition.
